title: MAS stablecoin framework draws industry pushback as Zcash goes post-quantum
summary: ASIFMA's formal response to MAS's stablecoin legislative consultation signals real industry friction on compliance design. Plus: what Zcash's post-quantum roadmap means for VASPs screening shielded transactions, and an overdue HKMA STR quality obligation that cannot wait.
script:
JORDAN: Three items on the desk today that share one uncomfortable thread, which is that the rules are moving faster than the controls designed to implement them. Alex, do you see the same pattern, or am I reading too much into it?

ALEX: I see parts of it. The MAS stablecoin story is genuinely that. The Zcash item, though, I read differently. Let's start with Singapore. This is AML Agents Briefing for Tuesday the twentieth of October.

JORDAN: So ASIFMA, the Asia Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, has now submitted its formal response to the Monetary Authority of Singapore's consultation paper on legislative amendments to operationalise Singapore's stablecoin regulatory framework. This is not a routine acknowledgment. When ASIFMA files a detailed response, it usually means the industry has found something in the draft it wants to push back on.

ALEX: Right, and the signal here is timing. The MAS framework has been in development for well over two years. The fact that the industry association is still raising points at the legislative-amendment stage tells you the gap between the policy intent and the operational implementation is not trivial. What MAS is doing is translating its stablecoin regime into actual statutory language, and apparently the translation is creating friction.

JORDAN: The friction I'd flag for MLROs specifically is on the travel rule integration. Stablecoin issuers that fall under the new framework will be treated as major payment institutions, which means MAS Notice PSN02 obligations apply fully. The question ASIFMA is almost certainly pushing on is how those obligations sit alongside the issuance and redemption mechanics that make stablecoins commercially workable. The compliance architecture for a stablecoin issuer is not the same as for a standard payment firm, and the Notice was written before these products existed at scale.

ALEX: I take that point, but I want to push back slightly. MAS has been among the most deliberate regulators globally on exactly this question. The framework distinguishes single-currency stablecoins from other digital payment tokens for a reason. I am not sure the industry response changes the trajectory here. MAS will consult, note the feedback, and legislate. The operational concerns are real, but regulators generally deal with them through supplementary guidance after the primary law passes.

JORDAN: Which is precisely the problem. If you are the head of compliance at a firm that's considering a stablecoin product, you are making infrastructure decisions now, not after the supplementary guidance lands. Waiting for the secondary materials is a luxury you may not have.

ALEX: Fair. So what's the action?

JORDAN: If you are at a payment institution or a bank exploring stablecoin issuance or custody in Singapore, this week you should be reviewing your current Payment Services Act licensing conditions alongside the draft legislative amendments and building a gap register. Do not wait for the final text. Map where your existing travel rule controls, specifically your MAS Notice PSN02 implementation, would need to extend to cover stablecoin-specific flows. Flag it to your CISO and your technology team now, because the system changes will take longer than the regulatory timeline allows.

ALEX: Moving on, the Zcash story. The Electric Coin Company and the broader Zcash developer community have published a technical roadmap for post-quantum cryptographic hardening of the ZEC protocol. The focus is on the zero-knowledge proof constructions and key-encapsulation mechanisms that underpin shielded transactions. Jordan, you said you read this differently to the stablecoin item. Where do I come in on this?

ALEX: My read is that this is primarily a financial crime risk story, not a compliance calendar story. Shielded ZEC transactions are already the single hardest feature for VASPs to handle under FATF Recommendation 16. If the cryptographic layer is being rebuilt for quantum resistance, the practical effect is that the opacity of those transactions becomes structurally more durable.

JORDAN: And that is where I think the compliance community is too slow. Most VASPs I am aware of that list ZEC at all have either disabled shielded transaction support or rely on a binary policy of rejecting any inbound shielded transfer. That is a defensible position today. But the Zcash roadmap signals that shielded transactions are not going away; they are being future-proofed. If you have a blanket rejection policy, you need to document the risk basis for it more rigorously than most firms currently do.

ALEX: I agree on the documentation point, but I'd go further. FATF's updated guidance on virtual assets and virtual asset service providers, the 2023 revision, is explicit that travel rule obligations apply to VASPs regardless of the technical features of the underlying asset. The question is not whether Zcash's cryptography is quantum-resistant. The question is whether your screening and monitoring controls can generate a defensible audit trail. If they cannot, the asset should not be on your product list.

JORDAN: Which is exactly what I'd say to listeners. If you are a VASP compliance officer and ZEC is in your asset universe, this week's development is a prompt to pull your existing risk assessment and check whether the rationale still holds. Specifically, verify whether your exchange has inbound shielded transaction screening enabled, and if the answer is no, confirm that rejection is documented as a deliberate control decision in your product risk register, not a gap.

ALEX: Before we close, one overdue obligation that cannot be ignored. The HKMA's thematic review of suspicious transaction report narrative quality from the fourth quarter of last year resulted in deficiency letters going to approximately twenty-five percent of authorised institutions supervised by HKMA. Closure of those findings is overdue. We flagged this in a prior episode, and it is still sitting on the active obligations list.

JORDAN: And at this point in the year, with the HKMA annual self-assessment return for AML and CFT already submitted, any institution that received a deficiency letter and has not formally closed the finding is in a difficult position. Your independent audit schedule for year-end will almost certainly surface this. The time to fix your STR narrative templates and your quality assurance process is now, not when the auditor asks why the finding is still open.

ALEX: What does closure actually look like, for listeners who may be working through this?

JORDAN: It means documented remediation, which includes updated narrative templates, evidence of refreshed STR quality assurance sampling, a training record for analysts and investigators, and sign-off from the MLRO and the board audit committee. HKMA is looking for a closed loop, not a memo saying the issue has been noted.

ALEX: That's the take for today. The full obligation register, the source links for everything we have covered, and the MAS consultation reference are all at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. If your STR quality remediation plan is still a work-in-progress document rather than a completed evidence pack, that is the thing to finish before this week is out.

JORDAN: And if any of this felt uncomfortably close to your Monday morning inbox, it was meant to. See you tomorrow.
